title: Question 5
stem:
An $\alpha$-particle is travelling in a vacuum towards the centre of a gold nucleus, as illustrated in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

The gold nucleus has charge $79e$.
The gold nucleus and the $\alpha$-particle may be assumed to behave as point charges.
At a large distance from the gold nucleus, the $\alpha$-particle has energy $7.7 \times 10^{-13} \text{J}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The $\alpha$-particle does not collide with the gold nucleus. Show that the radius of the gold nucleus must be less than $4.7 \times 10^{-14} \text{m}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about energy changes as the alpha-particle moves in. Far away all its $7.7 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$ is kinetic, but what happens to its speed as repulsion slows it down toward the nucleus?

Hint 2: At the point of closest approach the particle momentarily stops, so all the initial kinetic energy has become electric potential energy $E_p$ between two point charges. Recall how $E_p$ depends on the two charges $79e$ and $2e$ and separation $r$.
Hint 3: Set the initial energy equal to the potential energy at distance $r$ and rearrange to find $r$. If no collision occurs, what does this tell you about the actual nuclear radius?
parts.proper_answer: At closest approach, $E_k \rightarrow E_p$: $7.7 \times 10^{-13} = Qq/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r$ with $Q = 79e$ and $q = 2e$, giving $r = 4.7 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$. Since there is no contact, nuclear radius $< 4.7 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the energy transfer**
Imagine the alpha-particle flying head-on at the gold nucleus. Both are positive so they repel. Far away the repulsion is tiny and the $7.7 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$ is almost all kinetic energy. As it gets closer it slows down, losing kinetic energy and storing it as electric potential energy in the two-charge system.

Step 2: **Use closest approach condition**
The nearest it could ever get is where it just stops for an instant before turning back. There kinetic energy is zero, so all the starting energy is now potential:
$$E_k = E_p = \frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$
Here $Q = 79e$ for gold and $q = 2e$ for an alpha-particle, with $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.

Step 3: **Calculate the separation**
Put the numbers in:
$$7.7 \times 10^{-13} = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^9)(79 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19})(2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19})}{r}$$
$$r = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^9)(79)(2)(1.60 \times 10^{-19})^2}{7.7 \times 10^{-13}} \approx 4.7 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$$
This is the centre-to-centre distance if it just touches. Because you are told it does not collide, the gold nucleus itself must be smaller than this distance.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Determine the acceleration of the $\alpha$-particle for a separation of $4.7 \times 10^{-14} \text{m}$ between the centres of the gold nucleus and of the $\alpha$-particle.

markscheme_points.text: distance of approach so radius less than this ; $a = \text{... m s}^{-2}$

hints: Hint 1: At a given separation the only horizontal force on the alpha-particle is the electrostatic repulsion from the nucleus. How are force and acceleration linked for the alpha-particle?

Hint 2: Recall that the repulsive force between point charges falls as $1/r^2$ and depends on the product of charges $79e \times 2e$. Also recall the alpha mass is about $4u$ where $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$.
Hint 3: Combine $F = Qq/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2$ with $F = ma$ to solve for $a$ at $r = 4.7 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$, checking direction away from the nucleus.
parts.proper_answer: $F = Qq/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2 = ma$ gives $a \approx 2.5 \times 10^{27}\text{ m s}^{-2}$ directed away from the gold nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the force**
The alpha-particle feels a huge electrostatic repulsion. For point charges Coulomb's law gives:
$$F = \frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$$
with $Q = 79e$, $q = 2e$ and $r = 4.7 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$. The force points away from the nucleus, so the acceleration will too.

Step 2: **Link force to acceleration**
Newton's second law for the alpha-particle is $F = m_{\alpha} a$. An alpha-particle has 2 protons + 2 neutrons, so $m_{\alpha} \approx 4u = 4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$. Hence:
$$a = \frac{1}{m_{\alpha}}\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$$

Step 3: **Put in the numbers**
$$F = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^9)(79 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19})(2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19})}{(4.7 \times 10^{-14})^2} \approx 16\text{ N}$$
$$a = \frac{16}{4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{27}\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
Enormous because the charge product is large, $r$ is tiny, and the mass is tiny. Direction is away from the gold nucleus along the line of centres.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
In an $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment, the beam of $\alpha$-particles is incident on a very thin gold foil.
Suggest why the gold foil must be very thin.

markscheme_points.text: interactions between nucleus and $\alpha$-particle can be studied ; large deflections with nucleus do not occur

hints: Hint 1: Think what would happen if an alpha-particle had to pass many layers of gold atoms - could you still tell that one large deflection came from one single nucleus?
parts.proper_answer: Foil must be very thin so each alpha-particle is scattered by at most one nucleus, avoiding multiple scattering which would obscure large-angle single-nucleus deflections.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why one layer matters**
You want to study the interaction with a single nucleus. If the foil were thick, an alpha-particle would be nudged many times by many atoms and lose energy, so a large deflection could be built up from many small ones. A foil only a few atoms thick makes multiple scattering very unlikely, so any large deflection observed must come from a single close encounter with one nucleus.
